questions.prompt: He often ____ his wife as his best friend.
questions.explanation: “Refers to A as B” means calls A by the name B. He calls his wife his best friend.

questions.prompt: I want to ____ that new language program for learning English while sleeping.
questions.explanation: “Try out” means test something to see how it works. The speaker wants to test the language program.

questions.prompt: It has been six years, ____, since I visited my hometown.
questions.explanation: “More or less” means approximately. The time since the visit is about six years.

questions.prompt: Keep plenty of coffee ____ because this is going to be a long meeting.
questions.explanation: “On hand” means available and ready for use. Coffee should be ready during the meeting.

questions.prompt: She ____ her supervisor, so she does not mind when he offers her suggestions.
questions.explanation: “Thinks highly of” means has a good opinion of. She respects her supervisor and welcomes his suggestions.

questions.prompt: Wherever the president goes, his bodyguards are close ____.
questions.explanation: “At hand” means nearby. The bodyguards stay close to the president.

questions.prompt: There is no rush, so you can ____ getting ready.
questions.explanation: “Take your time” means proceed slowly and without rushing.

questions.prompt: This computer is ____ at this price. You should buy it before the sale finishes.
questions.explanation: “A steal” means a very good bargain. The sale price is especially low.

questions.prompt: We had to study most of the material ____ because the professor only wanted to talk about his theory in class.
questions.explanation: “On our own” means without help. The students had to learn the material independently.

questions.prompt: You will never ____ if you don't rest and do as the doctor says.
questions.explanation: “Get better” means improve or recover. Rest and following medical advice help recovery.

lines.speaker: Mark
lines.text: I think I'm ____. At least I can move my fingers today.
lines.explanation: Mark is improving physically. Use “getting better” after “I’m.”

lines.speaker: Bob
lines.text: Great! Everyone ____ the doctor who is treating you. They say he is the best.
lines.explanation: Everyone has a good opinion of the doctor. “Everyone” takes the singular verb “thinks.”

lines.speaker: Mark
lines.text: Yeah. He is good. I heard the nurse ____ Dr. Miracle.
lines.explanation: The nurse called the doctor “Dr. Miracle.” After “heard the nurse,” the base verb “refer” fits.

lines.speaker: Bob
lines.text: Well, everyone at work is hoping you can come back soon, but ____. Do you know how long you will be in the hospital?
lines.explanation: Bob tells Mark not to rush his recovery.

lines.speaker: Mark
lines.text: Actually, I am going home tomorrow. And since my wife has to work, I'll be ____ there all day.
lines.explanation: Mark will be alone at home without his wife’s help during the day.

lines.speaker: Mark
lines.text: I think so. I can manage things with my left hand ____.
lines.explanation: “More or less” means approximately or almost. Mark can manage, although perhaps not perfectly.

lines.speaker: Bob
lines.text: If you need anything, just call. I'll be close at hand. I'll come over and give you a hand. Just hand over all your problems to me. I can handle them. I'll be on hand.

lines.speaker: Mark
lines.text: OK! OK! I get it. Very funny! Thanks, Bob!

story.title: Idioms in context
paragraphs: My Brazilian friend has only lived in the United States for six months, but his English is great. Before he came to the US, he studied in a language school, but mostly he learned English on his own from reading English books and watching movies. He had learned basic conversation before he arrived in the US. Then, after he got here, his vocabulary and listening got better very quickly. I would say that he is now more or less fluent in English. However, sometimes he still has trouble with idioms.

One day, he asked me to help him buy some jewelry for his girlfriend back in Brazil. Her birthday was close at hand and he wanted to get something nice. He showed me a picture of his girlfriend before we went shopping. When I saw the picture I said, “Wow! Your girlfriend is a real spring chicken.”
My friend asked me, “Why do you refer to my girlfriend as a chicken?” I explained to my friend, “I just mean your girlfriend is very young and beautiful.”

At the jewelry store, they had several very nice necklaces on hand. I suggested that we take our time and look at several stores, but my friend found a diamond necklace that was a steal. He called the saleswoman over to buy it.

As the saleswoman was taking out the necklace, my friend decided to try out the new idiom he learned. He showed the saleswoman the picture of his girlfriend and asked, “Don’t you think she is a chicken noodle?” My friend’s English may not be perfect, but I still think highly of it.
